# Another Life — full site text
Updated 2026-10-16

# Another Life
URL: https://another-life.dk/

Made for this life. And another.
Hospitality furniture from teak that already lived once. Designed in a Danish tradition, made by hand in Indonesia, and built to stay in use for decades.
Watch the film · 0:34See the SATU collection
Another Life · Film · 0:34Close
Why we existHotels want Danish design. Then they fill the room with plastic.
Most hospitality furniture is bought, used for a few years and thrown away. We think the places that care most about how they look should also care how long their furniture lives.
So we start with teak that has already lived once, often in old joglo houses. We design every piece to ship flat, bolt together on site and be repaired part by part.
Our mission
Lounge Chairs on a garden terrace, styled for the shoot.
Second livesOur wood has stories.
Before it was furniture, our wood held up houses, carried people across rivers and rode the waves. Where our wood comes from
Once a family home in Java
Teak pillars that held up a joglo for generations, now holding up your guests.
Once a bridge over a river
Wood that carried people across the water for decades.
Once a fishing boat
Wood that rode the waves, now taking it easy by the pool.
Another material. Another owner. Another place. Another life.
Teak that already lived once, made into furniture that can outlast the room it was bought for.
Furniture worth keeping.
CollectionSATU. Seven pieces, one system.
Satu is Indonesian for one. Our first collection shares one material, one finish and one way of building: knock-down, bolted and repairable.

How we buildThree things every piece does.
01 / 03
01Reclaimed
Teak that already lived once, often in old joglo houses. Far too good to waste.
02Burned and oiled
An old Japanese technique, moved to a harder wood and a hotter climate. Finished with natural oil.
03Made to be rebuilt
Ships flat, bolts together on site and comes apart again whenever it needs to.
Our missionReuse beats recycling.
A bottle that gets refilled does more good than one that gets melted down. Furniture works the same way: the longer a piece stays in use, the less needs to be made again.
That idea shapes everything we design, and where we want to go next.
Read our mission
Work with usFurnishing a place?
We work with boutique hotels, resorts, restaurants and cafés, and with the architects and designers who furnish them. Tell us about the space and we'll reply with what is possible.
EnquireHow we work

# SATU Collection
URL: https://another-life.dk/collection.html

Collection
SATU
Our first collection. Seven pieces in one material, one finish and one way of building.
Satu means one in Indonesian. One material, one system, one idea carried through every piece. The collection is made from repurposed teak, timber that has already lived a life, often in old joglo houses, and given another through Danish design and Indonesian hands.
Every piece is modular and knock-down. It travels flat, comes apart without damage, and goes back together as it was. If one part reaches its end, only that part is changed.
The surface is finished with Shou Sugi Ban: the teak is darkened with flame and finished with natural oil. What is left is the material itself: honest, tactile, and made to age well.
Old wood, new purpose, long life.
Last updated 2026-10-16
01The ChairDining rooms, restaurants and terracesH 80 / W 45 / L 45 cm02The Sun LoungerPoolside and outdoorsH 32 / W 75 / L 211 cm03The BenchDining tables, terraces and hallsH 45 / W 206 / L 40 cm04The Lounge ChairLounges, lobbies and terracesH 78 / W 68 / L 60 cm05The Side TablePoolside, terraces and loungesH 32 / W 75 / L 75 cm06The Coffee TableLounges, lobbies and terracesH 32 / W 75 / L 100 cm07The TableDining rooms and restaurantsH 75 / W 100 / L 220 cm
Shared by every pieceOne design. Different lives.

# The Chair — SATU
URL: https://another-life.dk/the-chair.html

SATU · 01 / 07
The Chair
A knock-down dining chair in repurposed teak. It travels flat, goes together on site and is designed to be repaired for decades rather than replaced.
The Chair from behind, showing the open backrest, the slatted seat and the bolt clusters on the back legs

SATU

Price
On request. Ex works, Indonesia
Shipping
Flat-packed, assembled on site
Enquire about The Chair
DetailsAbout The Chair.
The first piece we designed, and the one the rest of SATU grew from.
The bolts are part of the look. Three-bolt clusters at the seat and leg joints hold the frame and let it be taken apart again.
Every component can be replaced on its own. A broken leg is a new leg, not a new chair.
Like every Another Life piece, it is made from timber that already had a first life. Marks from that life stay visible, wherever they don't reduce strength. And if a part ever wears out: replace the part, not the piece.
In detailBlack-and-white studio photograph of an earlier version of The Chair, showing the tapered legs and the three-bolt clusters at the seat jointsClose-up of The Chair's backrest and seat frame, with the burned grain and the bolt cluster visible
Black-and-white photograph of bare legs standing on The Chair at the edge of shallow water on a salt flatThe Chair from behind on a dark sand beach at dusk, the sea and a cloudy sky beyond
The Chair in profile on the same beach, the three-bolt clusters catching the evening light
Another Life PassportIts own story, one scan away.
We are building a tracing system that gives each piece its own QR code and its own story: where the wood of The Chair lived before, who made it, and how to care for it and repair it.

# Another Life Mission
URL: https://another-life.dk/mission.html

The best day was yesterday. Let's make sure there's a tomorrow.
Mission
On this page
Not needing to recycle · Why we exist · Origin · Beliefs · Design · Where we're heading
Last updated 2026-10-16
Our point of viewThe best kind of recycling is not needing to.
Think of an old glass milk bottle.
It gets returned, washed and refilled. Again and again. But take it out of that cycle, melt it down and make something new, and you've used energy to replace something that was already working.
We believe furniture should follow the same thinking. Keep materials and products in use for as long as possible.
Downcycling something that could continue to be reused isn't a step forward. It's a step backward.
PurposeWhy we exist.
To make furniture that lasts a long time.
Hotels and restaurants spend years building a sense of place, and many of them look to Danish design for credibility. Then they furnish those places with pieces that won't last: plastic chairs and loungers that are bought, worn out and replaced on a short cycle.
That gap is the reason Another Life exists. We make furniture that earns the design it borrows from: well made, built from material that already exists, and designed to be repaired rather than thrown away.
The new luxury is not newness. It is something you can keep.
The name
ANOTHER — LIFE.
The name is a belief. Old material deserves a second chance, and so does the furniture we make from it. A piece should be able to change hands and places many times and keep going.
Always written with the dash.
OriginA family company, born in Bali.
The family behind Another Life.
We moved to Bali partly for Green School. Its ethos, to do better, stayed with us, and it is why this company exists.
We wanted to build something that does good and still lets us live a healthy family life, rather than chase scale for its own sake. The idea came from looking around: hotels across Bali and the islands east of it, full of plastic furniture with short lives.
Another Life was founded by Stine Palm and Magnus Palm, and it is a family company. We build it the way we want to live: for the long run.
BeliefsWhat we hold to.
Luxury is longevity
The most valuable piece of furniture is the one you never need to replace.
Use it again first
Reuse before recycling. Recycling is the last stop, not plan A.
Reclaim first
We use timber that already exists before we look for anything new.
Design for repair
Joints are bolted. Parts can be replaced. Pieces are made to be passed on.
Say what we know
We tell you what is and isn't sustainable about a piece. A label alone doesn't settle it.
Every decision matters
There is no perfectly sustainable piece of furniture. There are better decisions, and we try to make them.
A conversation in a chair
Furniture should give the person sitting in it something to ask about, not only give the owner something to point at.
Design principlesDanish design, made where the material is.
Our design follows a Scandinavian tradition: simple, functional, made to last and to never go out of style. The pieces are made by hand in Indonesia, close to the timber and the people who work it.
Sketches, drawings and a burned sample on the design table.
Knock-down
Every piece ships disassembled and bolts together on site. Flat furniture takes far less space to move than assembled furniture.
Reassemblable
Joints must survive being taken apart and put back together many times, not once. A hotel can move, store or reconfigure its furniture.
Modular
Each component can be replaced on its own. One design can take different materials and parts over time, like a system rather than a single object.
Honest material
Grain, age, marks and imperfections stay visible. We want each piece to look like it has a story.
Where we're headingPlant. Give back. Collaborate.
We're just getting started, and we have big plans. We haven't planted a forest yet, and we won't pretend we have. But here's where we're heading.
Feet in the sand, eyes on what comes next.
Plant
For the wood we use, we want to plant new trees, including slow-growing native species like teak and ulin.
Give back
We want to share what we build with the communities behind our furniture: the makers we work with and the places the wood comes from.
Collaborate
We're looking for partners who share the idea: planting projects, NGOs, hotels, architects, makers and community initiatives.
Running a planting project, a community initiative or a hotel that wants to do better? Say hello. We love a good collaboration.
Work with us

---

# Material and Making
URL: https://another-life.dk/material.html

Material and making
Timber that already lived once.
Where our wood comes from, the ironwood we're developing, how we burn and oil it, and how every piece is built.
On this page
Where our wood comes from · Ironwood · Shou Sugi Ban, our way · Natural oil · Making · Hardware · The sign · Built to be rebuilt · Shipping
Last updated 2026-10-16
Chapter 1 · Where our wood comes from17,000 islands, built in wood.
Old wood waiting outside the workshop.
Indonesia has more than 17,000 islands, and for centuries much of it was built in wood. On Java, families lived in joglos: big teak houses held up by four mighty pillars and put together without a single nail.
Today many of them are making way for concrete. The teak inside is often older than our grandparents. Throw it away? Not on our watch. We'd rather give it another life.
Our teak (Tectona grandis) is repurposed: timber that has already lived a life, often in old joglo houses, and also in bridges, boats and other structures. We are also building a way to trace each piece's own story: the Passport.
Old posts and beams, marked and sorted before they are cut.
Reclaimed? Not always.Ask where it stood.
“Reclaimed” is one of the easiest words to put on a label, and one of the hardest to check. It matters, because a new tree is never just one tree.
What a new tree sets in motion
01The licence
A permit to take the biggest, oldest trees. On paper, the forest stays.
02The road
Roads are cut in to reach them. On Borneo alone, about 270,000 km of logging roads were built between 1973 and 2010. That's almost seven times around the Earth.
03The thinning
What's left is weaker: drier, poorer in wildlife and quicker to burn.
04The new label
Logged land can be reclassified for plantations. That's when the forest really goes.
05Gone
One crop, in rows. By 2010, plantations covered about a tenth of Borneo.
Swipe to see all five steps.
Reuse, in one numberUp to 92%
Lower emissions when a building is made from reused products instead of new ones.
From a 2024 study of a wooden house in the journal Buildings. Savings ranged from 23% to 92%, depending on how much was reused. It measured a building, not our furniture, but the logic is the same: what already exists does not need to be made again.
Our woodSets none of this in motion.
A joglo: the Javanese teak house much of our wood comes from.
The tree was felled generations ago. The wood has already done one job, holding up a house, a bridge or a boat.
But don't take our word for it. With us, you can check:
Where it stood: the building it came from.
What came with it: the records for its batch.
Which piece it became: the code on the furniture.
Open an example passportHow the Passport works
Sources: Gaveau et al., Four decades of forest persistence, clearance and logging on Borneo, PLoS ONE 2014 · Gaveau et al., Reconciling forest conservation and logging in Indonesian Borneo, PLoS ONE 2013 · Carbon assessment of a wooden single-family building, Buildings 2024
Chapter 2 · In developmentMeet ulin, Borneo's ironwood.
Reclaimed ulin: weathered outside, warm and dense inside.Old ulin beams. The S-shaped irons keep the ends from splitting.
Ulin (Eusideroxylon zwageri) is so dense it sinks in water, so tough that termites give up, and so slow-growing that a tree can live for more than a thousand years. For generations it carried fishing boats, held up bridges and kept river villages above the water.
A wood like that should never be cut new. So when an old boat or bridge retires, we give its ironwood a second career. Our first ironwood samples have just left the workshop.
Why can't you just buy new ulin?
Because a tree that takes centuries to grow was cut much faster than it could grow back. Indonesia stepped in: new ulin can no longer be exported, and the species is protected. Old ulin is another story. When a bridge, a house or a dock has done its job, its wood can start again, traced and documented. That's the only ulin we'll ever use.
Chapter 3 · Shou Sugi Ban, our wayFire, borrowed from Japan.
Burning the surface of the timber.
In Japan, carpenters have protected cedar by setting it on fire for centuries. Really. It's called yakisugi, and a charred surface helps wood stand up to weather and bugs.
We borrowed the idea and tried it on something harder: repurposed teak. We burn the surface, then rub in natural oil. The idea is to help the wood handle the tropical sun.
An old Japanese technique, moved to a new wood and a new climate. Just the wood, a little braver.
Chapter 4 · Natural oilInto the wood, not on top of it.
Old nail holes and marks stay part of the board.
Many outdoor finishes are coatings: a layer that sits on top of the wood. Over time they weather, flake off and end up in the soil and the sea.
We finish with natural oil instead. It soaks into the wood rather than forming a skin, and when a piece needs care, you oil it again.
Reclaimed wood also carries marks from its first life. They stay visible, wherever they don't weaken the piece. Character is welcome. A weaker chair is not.
MakingMade in Indonesia.
Every piece is made by hand in Indonesia by makers we work with directly, in small batches.
Producing close to the material keeps the supply chain short and visible.
Stacks of repurposed teak, drilled one board at a time.
The hardwareBolts built to outlive the chair.
Three holes, three bolts, at every main joint.
Hardware is usually the last thing anyone thinks about. It is often the cheapest part of a piece of furniture, and the first to fail: screws rust, threads strip, and a good chair is thrown out because of a part that cost almost nothing.
We turned that around. Every SATU joint is held by engineered stainless steel (SUS) bolts that screw into threaded inserts set into the wood. The bolt never cuts into the wood itself, so a joint can be opened and closed again and again without wearing out.
The three-bolt clusters you see on every piece aren't decoration. They hold everything together, and they're designed to last longer than the furniture around them.
The bolt.The insert it screws into.
The sign in the boltsThree dots. One circle.
Look closely at any SATU joint and you'll find three bolts. They hold the piece together, and they also carry the idea behind the name. Each bolt stands for a life the piece can have, and together they turn in a circle:
Material
The wood already lived once, before it reached our workshop.
Owner
The piece can move on to someone new and keep working.
Place
Undo the bolts and it can be rebuilt somewhere else.
Round and round, never ending. That's another life.
Built to be rebuiltFlat, bolted, and back again.
Parts fit by hand, then bolt together.
Every piece travels flat and is bolted together on site.
The same bolts let a piece come apart again without damage: to move it, to store it, or to change a single worn part while the rest carries on.
Prices are ex works, Indonesia.
ShippingStop shipping air.
An assembled chair is mostly empty space: between the legs, under the seat, behind the backrest. Ship it like that and you pay to move air across the ocean.
Flat-packed, a 40 ft high-cube container holds around 1,300 of our chairs, against roughly 350 assembled. Almost four times as many chairs per trip, so fewer containers, less fuel and a lower cost for every chair.
Our estimates. The final figures depend on packaging and loading.
20 ft40 ft high-cube
Flat-packed · ~1,300Assembled · ~350
Drag the slider to compare. Illustration.

# Another Life Passport
URL: https://another-life.dk/passport.html

Another Life Passport
A story you can scan.
We're building a system that gives every piece its own story: from the life its wood lived before, to every life it lives next.
One small code on the furniture. One page behind it. A story that keeps growing as the piece is used, repaired and passed on.
Last updated 2026-10-16
How it worksFrom one code to a whole story.
These are real screens from the Passport. Scroll to follow one batch of benches from the engraver to a guest's phone.
01 / 05
01MarkedOne code on every piece.
The system creates a batch code and a QR code, ready for the engraver. The code under the QR is a backup anyone can type in.
02ScannedA guest points a phone at it.
No app. The camera opens the page for that piece, with the batch code at the top.
03Its livesThe whole story in a minute.
From a teak tree, to the house, bridge or boat it held up, to the workshop, to the room it stands in now.
04Its journeyHow far it travelled.
Its route from the workshop, step by step, with an estimate of the transport CO₂ for that piece.
05Its careSomething loose? Tell us.
A short form with a photo comes straight to us, so a small repair keeps the piece in use.
Try itScan the code at the top of this page, or open the example.
Open the example passportFind a piece by its code
Beyond the labelA label is not a mission.
A stamp on the wall. Only part of the story.
We believe sustainability is a responsibility, not a certification.
We don't believe one label can tell the whole story. A certification can tell you where a material comes from, but not necessarily how long a product will last, how it was made, whether it can be repaired, or what happens when its life comes to an end.
Certifications have their place. But we've learned that a stamp of approval doesn't always mean a product is truly sustainable, and we believe sustainability should go much further than meeting a set of requirements.
We don't want to buy our way into being called sustainable. We want to earn it through the things we make. By questioning materials. By understanding their origins. By designing for longevity, repair and reuse. By taking responsibility for what happens long after a piece leaves our hands.
That's what the Passport is for: showing the evidence, piece by piece, instead of asking you to trust a stamp.
We don't claim to have all the answers. We're learning, questioning and challenging the way things have always been done.
Sustainability isn't a label you put on a product. It's a responsibility you build into it.
For hospitalityA story guests can read for themselves.
Hotels and restaurants are asked more and more what their spaces are made of, and furniture is often left out. The Passport is designed to give every piece a traceable origin, with something real behind it.
And it starts conversations. A guest scans a chair and reads that its wood once held up a family home in Java.
After the first lifeBuilt to support what comes next.
These are the services we're developing, and the Passport is designed around them.
A chair on the workshop floor, before it is burned.
Replacement parts
A single component, replaced on its own.
Refinishing
A worn surface brought back.
Reconfiguration
Parts rearranged for a new space or use.
Refurbishment
A full restoration of a used piece.
Take-back
Pieces returned to us and given another life, rather than discarded.
Build it with usWant to help shape it?
We're looking for hotels, designers and partners who care about where things come from and where they go next. We'll share more as the system takes shape.
Made from what came before. Made for what comes next.

# Another Life Questions
URL: https://another-life.dk/faq.html

Questions
Questions, answered plainly.
Last updated 2026-10-16
What is Another Life?
Another Life is a hospitality furniture brand from Bali. We make furniture from repurposed teak, designed in a Danish tradition, shipped flat and built to be kept for a very long time.
Where is Another Life based?
The company is based in Bali. Every piece is made by hand in Indonesia.
Who founded Another Life?
Stine Palm and Magnus Palm. It is a family company, and the idea was born in Bali, where the family moved partly for Green School.
What does the name mean?
The teak we use has already lived one life, in a house, a bridge or a boat. Every piece we make from it is meant to keep going: repaired, moved and handed on to its next owner.
What is SATU?
SATU is our first collection: The Chair, The Sun Lounger, The Bench, The Lounge Chair, The Side Table, The Coffee Table and The Table. The name is the Indonesian word for one, because every piece shares the same wood, finish and way of building.
What is the furniture made from?
Repurposed teak: timber that has already lived a life, often in old joglo houses. We give it another life through Danish design and Indonesian hands.
What is Shou Sugi Ban?
Shou Sugi Ban, or yakisugi in Japanese, is a centuries-old technique of charring wood with flame. In Japan it was made for cedar, a softwood. We use it on a hardwood, repurposed teak: we burn the surface, then finish it with natural oil. The result is a deep black colour and a texture you can feel.
Why do you burn a hardwood?
Because we wanted to see what an old Japanese idea could do for teak in the tropics. Charring gives the surface a protective, characterful skin, and the idea is to help the wood handle strong sun. We finish it with natural oil, which soaks into the wood instead of sitting on top as a coating.
What is a joglo?
A joglo is a traditional Javanese house: a tall roof carried by four big teak pillars, put together with joinery so it can be taken apart and moved. Many old joglos are making way for concrete houses. Much of the teak we use comes from houses like these.
What is ulin?
Ulin, or Borneo ironwood (Eusideroxylon zwageri), is one of the hardest woods in the world. It is so dense it sinks in water, and it built boats, bridges and piers for generations. It grows very slowly and is protected, so new ulin can no longer be exported from Indonesia. We work only with reclaimed ulin, traced and documented. Our first ironwood samples are made, and it is in development as our second material.
Why does every piece look a little different?
Because the teak has a history. Marks and nail holes from the wood's first life are part of its character, and we keep them visible as a quiet record of where it has been. Strength always comes first, so each piece is built to last.
Is Another Life furniture sustainable?
Sustainability guides every decision we make: repurposed teak, a flame-darkened finish with natural oil, flat-pack shipping, and furniture designed to be repaired rather than replaced. We believe the most sustainable piece is the one you keep for decades, so that is what we make.
How do you show where the wood comes from?
Today we tell it as the story of our wood: old houses, bridges and boats across Indonesia. We are also building the Another Life Passport, a QR tracing system that gives every piece its own story, from its first life to its next.
What happens when a hotel no longer needs the furniture?
It comes apart. Undo the bolts and every piece packs flat, can be stored, and goes back together for its next place or owner. If a part is worn, you replace that part, not the piece. Our furniture is made to be used, never stacked in a corner, and never sent to landfill.
Is the furniture recyclable?
It is solid wood finished with natural oil, so at the very end of its life it can be. But we hope it never gets there. Recycling ends a product's life and takes energy to make something new. We would rather a piece is kept, repaired, moved and passed on, like a glass bottle that is refilled instead of melted down.
Do you plant trees?
It is part of our mission. We want to plant new trees for the wood we use, give back to the communities and makers behind our furniture, and do it with partners who care about the same things. We have just started, so we say it as a goal, not as something we already do. If you run a planting or community project, we would love to hear from you.
Can the furniture be used outdoors?
Yes. It is made for hospitality spaces indoors and out, from dining rooms and lobbies to pools, terraces and gardens.
How is the furniture shipped?
Flat-packed. Every piece travels knocked down, so more fits in each container, and it is bolted together on site.
What holds the furniture together?
Stainless steel bolts, three at every main joint, screwed into threaded inserts in the wood. Hardware is often the weakest, cheapest part of furniture. We made it one of the strongest, so the joints can be taken apart and tightened again for decades.
Can the furniture be repaired?
Yes, and that is the heart of the design. Parts are bolted together, so any single part can be replaced and the piece goes straight back into service. It can be taken apart and put back together again and again.
What is the Another Life Passport?
The tracing system we are building. A small QR code on the furniture opens the story of that piece: where its wood came from and what it was before, who made it, how it travelled, and how to care for it and repair it. When a piece moves to a new owner, its story moves with it. We will share more as the system takes shape.
Who do you make furniture for?
Boutique hotels, resorts, restaurants and cafés, and the architects and interior designers who work with them. We love working with the people who shape what a place stands for.
Is Another Life Danish?
Yes. Another Life is a Danish family company. Design runs in the family: we come from a line of architects and furniture makers, and that heritage shapes everything we draw. We are Danish at heart and inspired by the world. Every piece is made by hand in Indonesia, close to the material and the makers.
How much does it cost?
We price every project individually, ex works Indonesia. Tell us about your space and we will come back with a proposal.
How do I order?
Send us a message with your space, the pieces you like and your timeline. We will reply with options, pricing and lead times.
